f: In March 2012 Greece swapped its privately held bonds at a loss of more than half their face value: the biggest sovereign restructuring in history.
In November 2011 Italy's 10-year yield averaged 7.06%. Silvio Berlusconi resigned as prime minister that same month.
Spain's 10-year yield averaged 6.79% in July 2012, the month Mario Draghi promised to do "whatever it takes" to save the euro.
Portugal asked for an EU-IMF bailout in April 2011. Its 10-year yield peaked at 13.85% in January 2012.
Ireland's banking collapse ended in an €85bn EU-IMF rescue in November 2010. Its yield peaked at 12.45% in July 2011.
Paul Volcker's Fed squeezed out inflation with record interest rates. The 10-year Treasury averaged 15.32% in September 1981, its all-time high.
h: The Fed squeezed out inflation with record interest rates, and the 10-year Treasury hit its all-time high.

f: On 16 September 1992, "Black Wednesday", the pound crashed out of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism.
h: The pound crashed out of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism, on a day traders still call Black Wednesday.

f: In September 1992 Sweden's central bank raised its overnight rate to 500% to defend the krona. It let the currency float two months later.
h: The central bank raised its overnight rate to 500% to defend the krona. Two months later it gave up and let the currency float.

f: In September 1992 the lira was forced out of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism, the same week as the pound.
The Fed's surprise hikes in 1994 caused the "great bond massacre": the 10-year Treasury went from 5.75% in January to 7.96% in November.
h: Surprise Fed rate hikes set off what traders called the great bond massacre.

f: The Bank of Japan announced negative interest rates in January 2016, effective in February. That month Japan's 10-year yield averaged below zero for the first time.
Japan's asset bubble burst in 1990. Its 10-year yield peaked at 8.03% in September 1990, then began a decades-long slide.
h: The asset bubble burst. The yield peaked, then began a slide that lasted decades.

f: In January 2015 the Swiss National Bank scrapped its cap on the franc. Swiss 10-year yields were negative in 59 of the 72 months from 2015 to 2020.
h: The central bank scrapped its cap on the franc without warning.

f: Germany's 10-year yield first averaged below zero in June 2016, the month of the Brexit vote.
The September 2022 "mini-budget" set off a gilt sell-off: the 10-year yield jumped from 2.33% in August to 3.50% in September, and the Bank of England stepped in.
In March 2020 the 10-year Treasury averaged below 1% for the first time, at 0.87%.
In October 2023 the 10-year Treasury averaged 4.80%, its highest monthly level since July 2007.
After François Mitterrand won the presidency in May 1981, capital fled France and its 10-year yield passed 17%.
h: A new Socialist president took office, and capital fled the country.

f: A currency crisis after New Zealand's 1984 snap election led to sweeping free-market reforms. Its yield peaked at 18.71% in May 1985.
h: A currency crisis after a snap election led to sweeping free-market reforms.

f: In September 1985 South Africa froze repayments on its foreign debt after banks pulled their credit lines.
The 1998 emerging-market crisis hit the rand hard. South Africa's 10-year yield averaged 18.30% in September 1998.
Canadian rates followed the Fed up. Canada's 10-year yield peaked at 17.00% in September 1981.
Hungarian inflation passed 25% in early 2023, among the highest in the EU. Its 10-year yield peaked at 10.25% in October 2022.
Poland joined the EU in 2004. Its 10-year yield fell from 11.86% in August 2001 to 4.72% in July 2005.
Greece adopted the euro in January 2001. By mid-2003 its 10-year yield was within 0.2 points of Germany's.
Italy's 10-year yield fell from 13.45% in March 1995 to below 5% by July 1998 as it raced to qualify for the euro.
In 1976 Britain borrowed $3.9bn from the IMF, then the largest loan the fund had ever made.
h: Britain borrowed $3.9bn from the IMF, then the largest loan the fund had ever made.

f: Ireland's 1980s debt crisis pushed its 10-year yield to 19.47% in February 1982.
Oil prices collapsed in 1986 and hit Norway hard: the krone was devalued by 12% in May 1986.
A banking crisis and the collapse of Soviet trade sank Finland's economy in 1991. The markka was floated in September 1992.
During the second intifada and a sliding shekel, Israel's 10-year yield reached 11.67% in October 2002. It peaked at 11.69% in February 2003.
The 2008 financial crisis pushed Mexico's 10-year yield to 9.82% in November 2008.
Chile's 2019 protests were followed by pension-fund withdrawals. Its 10-year yield rose from 2.70% in August 2019 to 6.34% in October 2021.
South Korea's 10-year yield fell to 1.25% in August 2019, then climbed to 4.27% in October 2022.
Slovenia's yield peaked at 6.90% in December 2011. In 2013 it rescued its own banks and narrowly avoided an EU bailout.
Australia floated its dollar in December 1983, ending decades of a managed exchange rate.
Inflation rose with the Vietnam War. In August 1971 Richard Nixon ended the dollar's convertibility into gold.
h: The president ended the dollar's convertibility into gold.

f: The 1973 oil shock pushed German 10-year yields above 10% in 1974, peaking at 10.8%.
Money poured into the franc in the late 1970s. In October 1978 the Swiss National Bank set a floor against the Deutsche Mark.
Spain devalued the peseta three times between September 1992 and May 1993.
Belgium's public debt passed 100% of GDP in the 1980s, one of the highest levels in Europe.
Until the 1980s Norway's interest rates were set by the authorities, not the market, and bank credit was rationed by quotas. That is why the line moves in steps.
Norway's 10-year yield peaked at 13.63% in December 1986, months after the oil-price collapse forced a devaluation of the krone.
In autumn 1982 Denmark fixed its exchange rate, banned wage indexation and tightened its budget. Long-term yields fell from 23.22% in September 1982 to 14.19% by April 1983.
h: The government fixed the exchange rate, banned wage indexation and slashed the deficit, and yields fell by 9 points in seven months.

f: In 1981 the Bank of Italy stopped having to buy the government bonds the Treasury could not sell, the so-called divorce. From then on the market set the price.
h: The central bank stopped having to buy the bonds the Treasury couldn't sell, the so-called "divorce."

f: From 1976 Austria tied the schilling to the Deutsche Mark, its hard-currency policy. It held until the euro replaced both.
In the 1970s Switzerland tried to stop money flooding into the franc by charging foreigners negative interest on their deposits. The franc kept rising anyway.
On 1 September 1998 Malaysia imposed capital controls and pegged the ringgit at 3.80 to the dollar, rather than turn to the IMF.
In December 2008 Latvia agreed a €7.5 billion rescue from the EU, the IMF, its Nordic neighbors and others. Its economy shrank by about 14% in 2009.
In March 2009 Romania secured a €20 billion rescue package from the IMF and the EU.
Bulgaria adopted the euro on 1 January 2026, becoming the 21st member of the euro area.
Croatia adopted the euro in January 2023, replacing the kuna.
In 1987 Japan's 10-year yield jumped from 3.78% in May to 6.10% in October, a bond-market rout in the middle of the bubble years.
In October 2008 Iceland's three biggest banks collapsed within a week.
Cyprus's March 2013 bailout made large bank depositors take losses, a first for the euro area.
In February 2015 Sweden's central bank cut its main rate below zero, to -0.1%.
In July 2012 Denmark's central bank became one of the first in the world to set a negative interest rate.
h: The central bank became one of the first in the world to set a negative interest rate.

f: In November 2016 Donald Trump's election win set off a bond sell-off. The 10-year Treasury rose from 1.76% in October to 2.49% in December.
h: A surprise presidential election result set off a bond sell-off.

f: In October 1979 Fed chair Paul Volcker announced, at a rare Saturday press conference, that the Fed would target the money supply. The 10-year yield jumped from 9.33% to 10.30% in a month.
h: A new Fed chair announced a radical policy shift at a rare Saturday press conference.

f: Greece held two elections in six weeks, in May and June 2012, with leaving the euro openly debated. Its 10-year yield climbed back to 27.82% in June 2012.
h: Two elections in six weeks, with leaving the euro openly debated.

f: In January 2015 the anti-austerity party Syriza won a snap election. In July 2015 voters rejected the bailout terms in a referendum. Greece's 10-year yield rose from 8.42% in December 2014 to 12.00% in April 2015.
h: An anti-austerity party won a snap election. Months later, voters rejected the bailout terms in a referendum.

f: Italy's new populist coalition took office in June 2018. That October the European Commission rejected its draft budget, a first for any member state, and Italy's spread over Germany reached 3.07 points.
h: A new populist coalition clashed with Brussels, and the European Commission rejected Italy's draft budget, a first for any member state.

f: On June 23, 2016, British voters chose to leave the EU. In August the Bank of England cut rates and restarted bond buying, and the 10-year gilt yield fell to 0.74%.
h: Voters chose to leave the EU. The Bank of England cut rates and restarted bond buying.

f: In May 1997, in its first week in office, the new Labour government handed control of interest rates to the Bank of England. The 10-year gilt yield fell from 7.64% in April to 7.17% in May.
h: In its first week, a new government handed control of interest rates to the Bank of England.

f: In October 1979 the new Conservative government abolished exchange controls that had been in place since 1939. The 10-year gilt yield rose from 13.09% that month to 14.76% in November.
h: The new government abolished exchange controls that had been in place for 40 years.

f: In December 2015 President Jacob Zuma fired his finance minister. Within a week South Africa had had three, and its 10-year yield rose from 8.49% in November to 9.63% in January.
h: The president fired the finance minister, and within a week the country had had three.

f: In February 1990 Chancellor Helmut Kohl offered East Germany a monetary union, months before reunification. Germany's 10-year yield jumped from 7.70% in January to 8.57% in February.
h: The chancellor offered East Germany a monetary union, ahead of reunification.

f: In January 1995, with Canada's 10-year yield above 9%, a Wall Street Journal editorial called the country an honorary member of the Third World. The next month's federal budget began deep spending cuts.
h: With yields above 9%, a Wall Street Journal editorial called the country an honorary member of the Third World. A deficit-cutting budget followed.

f: In June 2024 President Emmanuel Macron called a snap election. In December 2024 the government fell in the first successful no-confidence vote since 1962. France's spread over Germany widened from 0.51 points in May to 0.83 in December.
h: The president called a snap election. Six months later, the government fell in the first successful no-confidence vote since 1962.

f: In April 2013 the Bank of Japan promised to double the money base in two years. Japan's 10-year yield dipped to 0.49% that month, then jumped to 0.88% in May.
h: The central bank promised to double the money supply in two years.

f: In 1994 a global bond rout met a Swedish budget deficit of over 10% of GDP. Sweden's 10-year yield rose from 6.84% in January to 11.24% in September.
h: A global bond rout and a budget deficit of over 10% of GDP.
